# Preface: The xv6 Philosophy for Machine Learning Systems {.unnumbered}

## The Loss of First Principles

In computer science education, operating systems reached a pedagogical crisis in the early 2000s. Commercial operating systems like Linux and Windows had grown to millions of lines of C code, crowded with backward-compatibility layers, device drivers, and obscure kernel macros. A student attempting to learn virtual memory by reading the Linux kernel would get hopelessly lost in thousands of lines of architecture-specific assembly before ever seeing a page table walk.

MIT solved this crisis by creating **xv6**, a modern reimplementation of Dennis Ritchie and Ken Thompson's Sixth Edition Unix. xv6 is a few thousand lines of clean C. It is small enough that a student can read the entire codebase in a single semester, yet real enough that it boots on RISC-V hardware, handles interrupts, manages multi-core processes, and runs a real shell.

Today, machine learning systems face the same crisis.

Production frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow have grown into colossal codebases spanning millions of lines of C++, CUDA, Python, and compiler backends. The core ideas (the recorded computation graph that makes backpropagation automatic, the stride arithmetic that makes a transpose free, the scaled dot product at the heart of attention) are buried beneath dispatch tables, binding layers, template metaprogramming, and distributed runtime boilerplate.

As a result, an entire generation of practitioners has been trained to treat machine learning frameworks as black boxes. We write `import torch`, stack layers like Lego bricks, call `loss.backward()`, and hope the GPU does not run out of memory. When training stalls, when gradients explode, or when memory bandwidth saturates, the developer is left guessing because they do not understand what happens beneath the Python API.

## Harvard's TinyTorch: The xv6 of Machine Learning Systems

Harvard's TinyTorch is to machine learning systems as MIT's xv6 is to operating systems. It is built on the belief that the only way to truly understand a machine learning system is to build one yourself.

Just as xv6 captures the essential soul of Unix, TinyTorch captures the essential soul of a modern deep learning framework:

1. **Transparency**: TinyTorch depends on NumPy for array storage and arithmetic and on nothing else. Every layer, every backward pass, every optimizer update, and every tokenizer merge is written in readable Python that a student can trace line by line. The listings in this commentary walk through those exact core functions, explaining the algorithms and systems invariants without artificial hand-waving.
2. **A systems point of view**: We do not treat tensors as abstract mathematical symbols. We treat them as bytes in memory, indexed by strides, and bound by how fast that memory can be read.
3. **Progressive disclosure**: You will not be overwhelmed with complex architectures on day one. You start with memory layout in Chapter 1, build forward and backward mechanics through Chapters 2 to 8, construct vision and language architectures in Chapters 9 to 13, and turn to performance in Chapters 14 to 20. Each chapter uses only what earlier chapters have taught.
4. **Real end-to-end execution**: Despite its size, TinyTorch is not a toy. By the end of this book, your framework will tokenize English text, train a convolutional network on images, generate text with a small GPT-style transformer, and speed up its own inference with quantization, operator fusion, and a KV cache. The milestone chapters measure those results and show you how.

## Who This Book Is For

- **ML engineers and systems builders** who want to understand how deep learning runtimes work under the hood, why certain operations stall on memory, and how accelerators execute tensor computations.
- **Students and researchers** who want a rigorous, hands-on path from deep learning theory to the systems software that runs it.
- **Software engineers moving into AI** who learn best by reading clean code and building systems from the ground up.

Let us step into the engine room and build a framework from scratch.
